newsitem.title: USA: Rubin repeats U.S. won't use dollar as trade tool.
newsitem.headline: Rubin repeats U.S. won't use dollar as trade tool.

text.p: U.S. Treasury Secretary Tuesday blamed the widening U.S. trade deficit largely on slow economic growth overseas and reiterated his opposition to the use of dollar depreciation to boost U.S. competitiveness.
"The thing we must not do is to use the dollar as an instrument of trade policy," he told CNN television's "Moneyline" program.
The Commerce Department reported earlier that the U.S. current account deficit widened 19 percent in the third quarter, to a record $47.96 billion.
"We are still growing at a good pace and have been for the last four years," Rubin said. "Much of the developed world has not been, and I think the trade deficit largely reflects that," he added.
He said that a strong dollar helps attract foreign capital to the United States, keeping down interest rates here.

Rubin brushed aside concerns that the big rise in foreign buying of U.S. Treasury bonds posed dangers for the United States. "It's a great tribute to the way that this country's economy is viewed and, I might add, the economic policies of this administration," he said.

Sales of Treasury bonds by China were rumored to have roiled the U.S. market last week, but Rubin said he did not know if that was the case. "I don't know that selling by the Chinese particularly contributed to volatility," he said.
The Treasury is scheduled to sell its first index-linked debt next month designed to protect investors against inflation.
Rubin said the first issue may be "relatively small" but he voiced optimism that the market will eventually grow very large.

The new Treasury debt will be linked to changes in the Consumer Price Index. A congressionally-appointed commission last week said the CPI overstates inflation by 1.1 percentage points per year and called for adjustments in the index.
Rubin though said he did not expect any such adjustments to have a big impact on the inflation-indexed debt that Treasury is planning to offer.
"I don't anticipate that it will have a significant impact with respect to inflation-indexed bonds," he said.
Turning to the stock market, Rubin again seemed to play down comments by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan last week that temporarily roiled world equity prices.
Greenspan said the central bank needed to be wary when "irrational exuberance" infected stock and other asset markets because that could end up doing damage to the economy.
Rubin said he did not think that Greenspan had suggested that the stock market was overvalued. "What he did was to raise a question," the Treasury chief said.
